From Neural Networks to Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs): A Research Journey Spanning Nearly a Decade!

Research is a continuous journey of learning, exploration, and connecting ideas across disciplines.

My journey in machine learning began in 2017 during my postdoctoral research at Hiroshima University, Japan, when I worked on my first machine-learning research paper, "Machine Learning Algorithm for Autonomous Control of Walking Robot." 

The work involved developing a supervised learning algorithm using Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), backpropagation, and real-time pressure sensor data, with experimental hardware implementation for autonomous walking robot control.

During my Ph.D., my research focused on Graphene Nanoribbon (GNR) interconnect materials and physics-based mathematical modelling. The primary objective was to investigate and improve VLSI circuit performance in terms of propagation delay, power consumption, and chip area through advanced interconnect modelling.

These two research directions may initially appear different, but they gradually inspired me to explore a broader question:

Can we integrate the governing principles of physics with the learning capabilities of neural networks to address complex problems across multiple engineering and scientific disciplines?

After years of research, mathematical exploration, and interdisciplinary discussions, this vision has gradually evolved into our current research on Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs).

The exciting aspect of PINNs is their potential to establish a meaningful connection between several disciplines, including:

Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence
Physics and Chemistry
Mathematics and Biotechnology
Civil and Mechanical Engineering
Electronics and Electrical Engineering

Our two recent research papers on Physics-Informed Neural Networks represent an important outcome of this long research journey. 

I believe that integrating physical laws, mathematical formulations, and data-driven intelligence can open new research opportunities beyond conventional disciplinary boundaries.

For me, research is not merely about publishing papers; it is about connecting knowledge developed over time and transforming it into solutions for interdisciplinary challenges.

The journey continues! Waiting for good miracles... wait and watch....

Investors don't read your deck. They scan it.

In the first pass, a deck gets seconds per slide. If the problem, the market and the ask aren't obvious at scanning speed, the details never get read at all.

That's why structure matters more than decoration. A workable founder deck answers, in order:

→ What's the problem, and who has it?
→ What's the product, shown simply?
→ How big is the market, honestly framed?
→ What traction exists so far — real numbers only?
→ Who's the team, and why them?
→ What are you asking for, and what does it buy?

I built a 13-slide pitch deck template around exactly that flow — problem, market, traction, the ask. Every slide is native, editable PowerPoint text and shapes (no flattened images), with a real editable chart and table, so you can change every number and word in minutes. It uses Fraunces and Inter, two free fonts that are native in Google Slides, so it opens cleanly there too.

A template won't raise money for you — nothing can promise that. But starting from a sound structure beats starting from a blank slide at 1 AM.

You have to pay an upfront retainer.

Some of the most valuable learning happens when we take time to listen to people who have walked and are walking the same path we find ourselves in.

I had the opportunity to attend the 25th WIMBIZ Annual Conference, themed "Rooted, Rising, Ready: Born in Africa, Built for the World."

Rooms like these are big pictures of possibilities for me, because my own path has never fit neatly into one box. I'm a Petroleum Engineer heading the subsurface department, I sit on boards in the banking, mining and beauty sector and Beyond all of that, I'm deeply passionate about living intentionally in Purpose and teaching others to do the same. Some days, carrying all of that can feel like a lot. But being in a room full of people who have built across different sectors reminded me that range is not a distraction from purpose. It can be part of it.

The conference brought together women and men with diverse experiences in business, leadership and enterprise. With speakers including Aliko Dangote, Tony Elumelu, Tara Fela-Durotoye, Dr Ndidi Okonkwo Nwuneli and Affiong Williams, there was an opportunity to hear from people who have built, led and contributed across different sectors.

I particularly value spaces like this because they allow us to step outside our usual routines and engage with ideas and experiences beyond our immediate circles. For me, that's often where clarity comes: away from the next deadline, listening instead of leading.

Building a career, leading an organisation or growing a business comes with its own demands. Sometimes, hearing how others have navigated their own paths offers a different perspective on the decisions we make and the possibilities ahead of us.

The conference theme also stood out to me. As Africans, we should be confident about the value of our roots, experiences and perspectives, while continuing to prepare ourselves for opportunities beyond our immediate environment. I spend my working days studying what lies beneath the ground, and I've learned that what's underneath determines what can rise. Our roots are not something to outgrow. They are what make us ready.

I'm glad I was part of this year's gathering. I look forward to taking the conversations and connections beyond the conference.

Engineers bring strong analytical rigor, structured problem-solving, and systems thinking into consulting. To move from technical execution to business strategy in 2026, focus on framing engineering work around cost, risk, revenue, and organizational impact.

1. Pick the Right Entry Niche

Start where your technical background gives you immediate credibility:
• AI & Implementation Consulting: Deploy and operationalize AI systems in production, manage human-AI workflows, and audit AI outputs.
• Cloud, SaaS & Security Advisory: Lead cloud migrations, multi-cloud modernization, enterprise software rollouts, and cybersecurity/compliance programs.
• Operations & Digital Transformation: Optimize supply chains, manufacturing, and business processes using data and systems thinking.
• Strategy & Generalist Consulting: Move into broader business strategy at firms like McKinsey, BCG, Bain, Deloitte, or PwC—often via campus hiring, an MBA, or experienced-hire routes.

2. Build Business Fluency

• Translate tech to ROI: Frame recommendations around cost savings, speed to value, risk mitigation, and stakeholder buy-in rather than technical elegance alone.
• Gain cross-functional exposure: Take on product, pricing, analytics, or transformation initiatives in your current role, or build business/finance fundamentals through coursework or an MBA.

3. Plan Your Timeline & Networking

• Set a realistic runway: Most users on Quora agree that career transition timelines typically span 6–12 months for smaller or internal consulting roles and 12–24 months for top-tier strategy consulting or MBA-led pivots.
• Network for referrals: Connect with engineers-turned-consultants, request informational chats, and target referrals rather than relying solely on cold applications.

4. Ace Consulting Interviews

• Case & structured problem-solving: Practice breaking ambiguous business problems into clear hypotheses, running quick math, and delivering concise recommendations.
• Behavioral & impact stories: Highlight leadership, stakeholder management, and measurable business outcomes from your engineering projects.

I was honoured to be invited by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Korea (MOFA) and the United Nations Office for Disarmament Affairs (UNODA) to speak and participate in the 25th ROK-UN Conference on Disarmament and Non-Proliferation Issues, held in Seoul on 12–13 November 2026.

This year’s theme was “The Multifaceted Impacts and Implications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on Disarmament, Non-Proliferation and Arms Control.”

🧬 Biosecurity and biological weapons

I delivered a presentation titled “Biosecurity and Bioweapons Prohibition in the Age of AI: Risks and Opportunities for Southeast Asia” during the panel on “AI and Chemical and Biological Weapons – Implications for Prohibition Regimes and Risk Reduction.”

I explored how AI can strengthen disease surveillance, outbreak preparedness, laboratory security and biological risk assessment, while also creating new dual-use and cyberbiosecurity risks. I highlighted the importance of ASEAN cooperation, responsible AI governance, stronger national biosecurity capacities and effective implementation of the Biological Weapons Convention (BWC). This is based on our biosecurity research program at RSIS | S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies . 

☢️ AI, nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation

I also had the opportunity to exchange insights on the implications of AI for nuclear disarmament and non-proliferation, particularly its potential impact on the implementation of key international instruments, including the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT), the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons (TPNW), and Nuclear-Weapon-Free Zone (NWFZ) treaties. Discussions considered how emerging AI applications could create new challenges and opportunities for treaty implementation, verification, monitoring, risk reduction and international cooperation.

🌐 Broadening the conversation on arms control

I was particularly delighted to see regional and international discussions on arms control and disarmament moving beyond traditional security insights. The inclusion of new-generation experts, greater attention to frontier technologies such as AI, and engagement with emerging actors from scientific, technological and private-sector communities are broadening the perspectives and expertise shaping disarmament conversations. This is essential to keeping arms control and disarmament frameworks relevant to a rapidly changing technological and security landscape.

🙏 My sincere thanks to MOFA of the Republic of Korea and UNODA for convening this important dialogue. It was a valuable opportunity to share research, exchange perspectives and explore how technological advances can be harnessed while safeguarding international peace and security.

Introducing CKCA Research OS Ω∞: Building the Architecture for Knowledge That Can Be Reconstructed, Evaluated, and Governed

What happens when human intelligence, artificial intelligence, institutions, research, and distributed knowledge must work together without losing context, provenance, accountability, or the ability to correct mistakes?

That is the problem I am addressing through CKCA Research OS Ω∞ — Constitutional Knowledge Coordination Architecture.

My work explores an architecture designed to coordinate knowledge across disciplines, intelligent systems, institutions, and knowledge holders while preserving the distinctions that matter:

• Research discovers.
• Evidence supports.
• Engineering implements.
• Evaluation verifies.
• Constitutional governance adopts.
• Stewardship preserves.

CKCA is organized around thirteen constitutional laws, five research tiers, fifteen lifecycle stages, and eight independent maturity dimensions.

Its foundational principles include:

Evidence Before Complexity.
Reconstruct Before Concluding.
Provenance by Default.
Context Before Generalization.
Disagreement Preservation.
Continuous Correctability.

The central proposition is straightforward: knowledge should not become institutional authority merely because an AI system generated it, a majority accepted it, or an organization repeated it.

Research findings and recommendations do not automatically authorize adoption or execution. Authority, evidence, decisions, and accountability must remain distinguishable.

I am currently developing the proposed v2.1 Draft 0.1 review through passage-level reconciliation, source attribution, and a separate review register. This is documentary architectural work—not a claim of completed implementation, certification, or institutional adoption.

I believe the next generation of intelligence infrastructure must do more than produce answers. It must preserve how conclusions were reached, what remains uncertain, who holds authority, and how decisions can be corrected.

The objective is not simply more intelligence. It is intelligence that can be examined, challenged, reconstructed, and responsibly governed.

— Created and developed by Dar-z Morris
November 19, 2026

📚 Week 19 | Systematic Literature Review: AI, Business Analytics & Decision-Making

Another milestone completed in my ongoing research project:

“The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Enhancing Business Analytics and Decision-Making: A Systematic Review.”

This week, I reviewed a 2022 research paper:

“Business Intelligence and Analytics (BIA) Usage in the Banking Industry Sector: An Application of the TOE Framework.”

The study explores how technological, organisational, and environmental factors influence Business Intelligence and Analytics adoption in the banking sector.


🔍 Key research insights:

Data-related and technology-supporting infrastructure play an important role in analytics adoption.
Top-management support and organisational champions encourage analytics implementation.
Employee capabilities and talent management are important organisational considerations.
Competitive pressure, external market influence, and regulatory compliance also influence BIA usage.

The study, based on responses from 120 employees at Arab Bank in Jordan, highlights that successful analytics adoption involves more than technology. Organisational readiness and external conditions matter too.



💡 My key takeaway:

Before organisations can benefit from advanced AI-driven analytics, they need the right technological infrastructure, capable people, management support, and an environment that encourages adoption.

This paper contributes supporting evidence to my research, particularly around organisational readiness and business analytics adoption. It does not directly evaluate AI techniques or measure improvements in decision-making quality.

The most dangerous thing about a good AI-generated implementation plan is how finished it looks.

Neat phases. Clean timelines. Every task assigned.

And buried underneath it are assumptions nobody has checked.

Does “customer” mean a contact or an account?
Can a deal have two owners?
What happens when the source system sends an empty value?
Who decides whether a duplicate should merge?

A plan that can't answer those questions isn't ready for a build.

I've started judging AI-assisted discovery by a different standard: did it uncover the decisions we were about to skip?

Use AI to draft the process map, sure.
But make it produce an assumptions register, conflicting definitions, and the questions that need a human owner.

A beautiful answer is easy to generate.
A useful question can save weeks of rework.

What's the requirement that usually gets discovered too late on your projects?

Patient expectations for artificial intelligence transparency and agency: A qualitative study and proportionate framework for clinical artificial intelligence implementation

AI is showing up across care, from ambient scribes to diagnostic support, but we know little about what patients expect when it is used. Most enterprise AI safety still relies on probabilistic guardrails—training models to “behave” or wrapping them in text filters.

In high-consequence systems, behavioral alignment cannot fix an architectural privilege problem. When an autonomous agent holds execution authority across retry loops, even a tiny per-attempt failure probability compounds into substantial cumulative risk (the Regeneration Gap).

The fix isn’t a smarter prompt filter. It’s separating proposal from permission:

Existence ≠ Permission.

When a human-AI cockpit can initiate real-world actions, its cognitive interface may adapt—but its permission boundary must remain independently enforced: D(a) = DENY ⇒ Δ_external(a) = 0.

An AI agent is software you give a goal. It works out the steps itself, using tools such as email, a CRM or search, and checks its own results as it goes.

Underneath, it runs on five parts: a model that reasons, tools it can call, instructions that describe the job, memory for what it needs to carry between steps, and limits on what it can do without approval. A hypothetical 12-person landscaping company shows the pattern: its agent reads a quote request, checks the price list and the crew calendar, drafts a quote, then rechecks the numbers before filing the draft for the owner to send.

Read access and the right to draft are a sensible starting point for any new agent. Write access gets earned once it has a track record on real work.

Welcome to Edition 8 of The SPAR Journal.

THE NEW SOCIAL CONTRACT FOR ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE:
Who owns productivity gains, who bears the costs, and what should society demand in return?

Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming part of the infrastructure through which the world works, learns, creates and makes decisions. Its development offers extraordinary possibilities, from scientific discovery and improved public services to stronger productivity and wider access to knowledge. Yet these opportunities arrive alongside profound challenges involving employment, inequality, security, human rights, environmental resources and the concentration of economic power.
These challenges cannot be understood solely through the interests of individual companies, industries or nations. AI crosses borders, draws upon humanity’s collective knowledge, and may produce consequences that extend far beyond the jurisdictions in which systems are developed. The world must therefore approach AI not only as a collection of competing economies, but as one interconnected human community.
This does not require every nation to adopt identical laws or political values. It requires a shared commitment to transparency, human dignity, scientific cooperation, accountability and the responsible management of risk. Governments, researchers, businesses, workers, and communities must work together to ensure that technological progress does not outpace society’s ability to govern it.
The future of AI need not be a choice between prosperity and protection. With cooperation, foresight and responsible control, humanity can pursue both. The greater tragedy would not be that AI became powerful, but that the world failed to work together to ensure its power served a common, peaceful future.

In this edition: Global political economy | Labour and productivity | AI control and technical safety | International governance | Taxation and social dividends | Legal responsibility

As artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in business operations, organizations are facing a challenge that extends well beyond technology implementation.

Are our governance practices evolving as quickly as our AI capabilities?

Businesses are increasingly relying on AI to support financial planning, operational decisions, customer engagement, and enterprise transformation. Yet many organizations continue operating with governance structures, decision-making processes, and accountability models that were never designed for increasingly autonomous technologies.

Throughout my experience leading enterprise technology and business transformation initiatives, one lesson has remained consistent: successful transformation requires more than implementing new capabilities. Strategy, business processes, people, and governance must evolve together.

Artificial intelligence makes that alignment even more important.

In Edition 03 of The Kingdom Advantage | Executive Leadership Briefing, I explore why AI governance must be an executive leadership responsibility, including:

1. Executive oversight: Establishing clear ownership and accountability for AI-enabled decisions.
2. Decision rights: Defining where technology can act independently and where human authorization remains essential.
3. Risk management: Aligning controls and monitoring with the potential consequences of AI-driven activities.
4. Organizational readiness: Ensuring leaders and employees understand their responsibilities as AI capabilities expand.

Effective governance should not be viewed as an obstacle to innovation. When designed thoughtfully, it provides the foundation for scaling technology responsibly while protecting organizational trust and creating sustainable business value.

The question is no longer simply what AI can do for our organizations, but whether we are prepared to lead and govern what it makes possible.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is one of the most transformative technologies of the modern era. It refers to the capability of machines and computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence, including learning, reasoning, problem-solving, language understanding, decision-making, perception, and creativity. AI has moved from a theoretical concept explored by researchers in the mid-20th century to a practical technology that influences nearly every aspect of modern life. Today, AI powers virtual assistants, recommendation systems, autonomous vehicles, medical diagnostic tools, financial forecasting models, and advanced generative systems capable of producing text, images, audio, and video. The rapid growth of AI has been fueled by advances in computing power, the availability of massive datasets, and breakthroughs in machine learning and neural networks. As organizations continue to integrate AI into their operations, the technology is increasingly becoming a fut

Anthropic’s upcoming IPO highlights the continued strong demand for AI and offers an opportunity to consider how companies can turn that demand into sustainable business results.

What interests me most is that AI is not one trade. It’s a value chain, from compute and infrastructure, to models and software, to the companies putting intelligence to work in real workflows.

Each link has different economics, different risks and a different timeline. Infrastructure may capture investment first. But over time, the bigger question may be where AI creates measurable productivity, stronger margins and lasting competitive advantage.

Where is adoption becoming real?
How quickly can it be monetized?

Which part of the AI value chain do you think investors find hardest to evaluate?

The goal of AI automation shouldn't always be to remove humans from the process. Sometimes, it's to help humans make better decisions.

Imagine a company implementing an AI-powered customer support system.

A customer raises a complaint involving a refund of ₹50,000.

Should the AI independently approve the refund?

I'd be careful.

Not every business decision should be fully automated.

This is where Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) becomes important.

Here's how I'd approach the workflow:

🔹 Step 1: AI analyses the request

Understand the complaint, identify the issue, and retrieve relevant order information.

🔹 Step 2: AI recommends an action

Suggest whether the case qualifies for a refund based on predefined policies.

🔹 Step 3: Human reviews the recommendation

A responsible employee checks the evidence and approves or rejects the decision.

🔹 Step 4: System records the outcome

Capture the decision for auditing, monitoring, and future process improvements.

As an AI Project Manager, I'd define:

- Which decisions AI can make independently.
- Which decisions require human approval.
- What confidence or risk thresholds trigger escalation.
- How decisions are logged and monitored.
- What happens when the AI cannot provide a reliable recommendation.

My takeaway: Good AI implementation isn't about automating every decision. It's about knowing which decisions should remain under human control.

The best solutions combine machine efficiency with human judgment.

💬 Where would you insist on human approval in an AI-powered business workflow?

🎙️ #ISPECTalks with Dr. Guillaume Fontaine: 701 Frameworks. Are We Asking the Right Questions?

Implementation science has developed hundreds of #theories, #models, and #frameworks. But are we using the right ones? And are they equipped to address the challenges health systems face today?

In this episode of #ISPECTalks, Dr. Guillaume Fontaine, Canada Research Chair in Implementation Science for Health Systems Transformation, Assistant Professor at McGill University, and Director of the RISE³ Implementation Science Lab | McGill University, joins Prof. Moriah Ellen to explore how implementation science can become more rigorous, more useful, and better equipped for a rapidly changing world.

From the identification of 701 theories, models, and frameworks to the development of the SELECT-IT meta-framework, Guillaume challenges us to think more critically about how we select and apply implementation science frameworks and how artificial intelligence might transform the field.

The conversation also explores an increasingly important question: Are our existing approaches fit for purpose in a world shaped by conflict, resource scarcity, misinformation, and rapid technological change?

A few of the standout takeaways:
🧩 The best framework is not necessarily the most widely used, but the one that fits your research questions, context, and capacity to apply it rigorously.
🎯 Evidence suggests that strategies intentionally matched to barriers and facilitators may produce more sustained improvements than approaches relying on education or audit and feedback alone.
🤖 AI offers exciting opportunities to understand complex contexts, synthesize evidence, and support decisions, but human oversight and careful evaluation remain essential.
🔬 Without stable, machine-readable definitions and relationships between concepts, AI risks applying our theories and frameworks inconsistently.
🌍 Why the future of implementation science depends on looking outward: Addressing today's health system challenges requires stronger connections with political science, sociology, economics, data science, and other disciplines, not simply developing more tools within our own field.

"The future of implementation science lives at the intersection of implementation science and other disciplines."

Machine Intelligence is a reproducible logical transformation process that discovers, resolves, and validates relationships through recursive reasoning.

Artificial Intelligence is a probabilistic mapping system that generates outputs from learned statistical relationships.

The distinction: Artificial intelligence predicts plausible responses. Machine intelligence derives logically reproducible resolutions.

Machine intelligence does not think independently or initiate its own objectives. It performs the analysis it has been instructed to perform, follows the logical transformations to resolution, and stops.

It does not require prior knowledge of the answer or complete comprehension of what it discovers. Its intelligence resides in the reproducibility of the logical transformation process.

Machine intelligence executes the reasoning it is directed to perform. It does not invent a reason to continue.

THE NEXT GENERATION OF RESEARCH: PERSONALIZED LEARNING, ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE, AND A PARADIGM SHIFT IN EDUCATIONAL LEADERSHIP
Building upon more than three decades of interdisciplinary scholarship, Dr. Adrianne Harrison-Surgeon's continuing research advances a critical question for the future of education: How can K–12 schools and higher education institutions effectively integrate artificial intelligence with personalized learning to transform instructional practices, strengthen educational accountability, and improve student success?
The next generation of educational transformation requires more than adopting emerging technologies. It demands a fundamental paradigm shift in educational leadership, institutional decision-making, instructional design, and collaboration with technology providers.
For decades, educational institutions have implemented reforms, introduced new instructional tools, and invested in technologies without consistently addressing the underlying structures and practices that limit student achievement. Continuing to apply the same approaches while expecting different outcomes is neither sustainable nor sufficient for meeting the needs of today's diverse learners.
The paradigm shift must begin at the highest levels of educational leadership.
School district administrators, university leaders, policymakers, researchers, and educators must move beyond serving as consumers of educational technology to becoming active collaborators in its research, design, development, implementation, and evaluation.
This transformation requires establishing meaningful partnerships with artificial intelligence technology providers at the earliest stages of conceptualization and product development, rather than waiting until technologies are fully developed and introduced into classrooms.
Teachers, educational researchers, and instructional leaders must have a voice in determining what AI-powered learning systems should measure, analyze, communicate, and adapt. Their professional expertise and classroom experiences are essential to identifying the instructional information educators need to make timely, informed decisions about individual student progress.

Personal branding is a lot simpler than you think.

Being invisible and being ignored have easy fixes.

And they only take 15 minutes a day.

If you know your stuff but nobody sees it, post.
If you post but nobody reacts, comment.

I spent 3 years on LinkedIn crawling to 3,000 followers.
The next 2 years took me to 100,000.

You probably think you don't have time.

But if you can scroll for 20 minutes at lunch, you have time for this.

Here's how I'd slot both into your week without it feeling like homework...

1. Comment before you post
↳ Leave 3 thoughtful comments on posts in your niche.
↳ Their audience meets you before they ever see your content.

2. Keep a "one idea a day" note
↳ Jot down one question a client asked you today.
↳ By the end of the month, that list is your content plan.

3. Turn a repeat question into a post
↳ Write up the answer you've given ten times this year.
↳ If clients keep asking, your audience wants it too.

4. Reply to every comment you get
↳ Each reply keeps the conversation alive under your post.
↳ People notice when a real person is behind the profile.

5. Write for a junior colleague
↳ Explain one thing you'd want them to know at 25.
↳ Simple language lands better than industry jargon.

6. Follow 10 people a step ahead of you
↳ Read how they open their posts and where they stop.
↳ Then notice which lines made you stop scrolling.

7. Save every hook that stops you
↳ Keep a swipe file of openers on your phone.
↳ Rewrite them in your own voice when you're stuck.

Bottom line, your expertise deserves an audience.

And 15 minutes a day is how you build one.

What's your 15-minute LinkedIn habit? 👇

Your profile should make three things obvious within seconds:

🚀 “Your LinkedIn Profile Is a Landing Page. Are You Tracking Conversions?”

Imagine spending hours creating content, getting thousands of impressions, and attracting hundreds of reactions.

Sounds successful, right?
But what if none of that creates a single meaningful professional opportunity?

As a digital marketer working with Google Ads, AI advertising, and performance analytics, I've learned one important lesson:

Visibility is not the same as value.

And I believe the same principle applies to personal branding.
Think about your LinkedIn presence as a marketing funnel:

🔎 Impressions — People discover your content.
👀 Profile views — They become curious about you.
🤝 Connections — They want to stay in touch.
💬 Conversations — Relationships begin to develop.
🚀 Opportunities — Trust turns into collaboration, referrals, or business.

Here's the interesting part.
A post with 20,000 impressions might generate plenty of attention but little lasting value.
Another post with just 500 impressions might reach exactly the right people and open an important door.

That's why I believe personal brand performance shouldn't be measured by how many people see you, but by how many of the right people remember, trust, and connect with you.

AI can help us create more content than ever before.
But publishing more doesn't automatically mean building a stronger brand.
The real competitive advantage is becoming someone people want to work with.

💡 My question to you:

If you had to choose, would you rather have 10,000 LinkedIn followers or 100 highly relevant professional connections?
And why?

My LinkedIn impressions dropped 41% in the last 90 days.
177,342 impressions, down from about 300,000 the quarter before.

I run a personal branding agency. I probably shouldn’t post this.

But here’s the rest of the funnel:

→ 177,342 impressions
→ 46,323 people reached (almost half of them don’t follow me)
→ 5,101 engagements
→ 201 people clicked through to our website
→ 30 discovery calls
→ 6 new clients

If I only looked at the first number, this was a bad quarter.
But this month alone, we have 10 clients in our pipeline.

Here’s what the analytics actually showed me:

1. Breakdowns and niche “how-to” posts got the most saves and brought the most leads.

2. One personal post a week builds distribution. Not generic motivation, but posts that show who you are, like a hobby (for me, it’s football). People feel they already know you when you meet offline or when you’re hiring.

3. Evergreen posts keep working. This quarter I was busy with sales and my team was busy with client delivery, so some of what we published was written five months ago. It still brought in leads. Write once and reuse. But you need a library of posts that have already proven themselves.

So for the next 90 days, I’m judging LinkedIn from the bottom of that list, not the top.
What’s the first number you check on your dashboard?

LinkedIn is not an online CV.

That's how I opened my talk on personal branding on LinkedIn, organised by BrandMe Agency.

A CV waits to be read.
A brand gets found.

Here's what I shared - and what you can try this week:

	1.	Pass the 5-second test.
Can a stranger understand what you do from your banner, headline and photo? If not, start there.
	2.	Pick 3 topics and stay with them.
People remember you when your name keeps showing up next to the same subjects.
	3.	Write from real experience.
One honest story from your work beats ten "thrilled to announce" posts.
	4.	Your comments are content too.
"Great insights, thanks for sharing!" is invisible. Add one line from your own experience, and people click your name.
	5.	Don't wait for the perfect photo.
A real moment from your desk, a site or an event works better than a polished one.

You don't need to influence everyone.
You need to be recognisable to the people who matter to your goals.

Thank you, Brand Me, for the invitation, and to everyone who came.

Which of these do you find hardest?

LinkedIn needs a ‘Would they say this if I wasn’t their client?’ button

Let me tell you why: 

Your agency writes and calls a post brilliant
On the other hand, your team calls you inspiring
Your friends comment, “Couldn’t agree more.”

Agree with what? 
The post went live 11 seconds ago.
(Now this is weird)

Sometimes your personal brand has a laugh track. The same people applaud every post, and eventually you start believing every thought deserves a TED Talk.

I run a personal branding company. I know how easily we can confuse a well-supported post with a well-written one.

We’ve discussed the idea on calls, read three drafts and explained the context to each other.

Of course it makes sense to us. We attended the entire production (damn)

The stranger scrolling past owes us none of that effort.

So when I review content, I want answers beyond ‘the engagement looks good’:

📍What are people responding to? 

20 ‘Congratulations’ comments tell me something different from 20 people discussing the actual argument.

📍Can someone explain the point without our help? 

If I need to send a voice note explaining the post, the post needs another draft.

📍Where did someone disagree or lose interest? 

Give me the exact sentence. ‘Amazing as always’ gives me absolutely nothing to work with.

Cheer for your people. I do too.

But if you’re paying me to build your personal brand, you should occasionally hear, “This isn’t good enough yet.”

Otherwise, you’ve hired a very expensive applause machine.

LinkedIn Optimization: Turn Your Profile into Your Personal Brand

In today's digital world, LinkedIn has become more than just a job-search platform. It is a powerful tool for building your professional identity, connecting with industry experts, and discovering career opportunities.

But simply creating a LinkedIn profile is not enough. How effectively does your profile represent you?

What Is LinkedIn Optimization?

LinkedIn optimization is the process of improving your profile to make it professional, attractive, and easily discoverable by recruiters and industry professionals.

5 Simple Ways to Optimize Your Profile

1. Professional Profile Picture: Use a clear photograph and an attractive banner to create a positive first impression.

2. Strong Headline: Highlight your skills, interests, current role, and career aspirations.

3. Engaging About Section: Introduce yourself by sharing your educational background, strengths, experiences, and goals.

4. Showcase Your Achievements: Add internships, certifications, projects, skills, and extracurricular activities.

5. Stay Active: Share your learnings, engage with professional content, and build meaningful connections.

Why Does It Matter?

An optimized LinkedIn profile helps improve your visibility, connect with recruiters, explore career opportunities, and build a strong personal brand.

Final Thoughts

Your LinkedIn profile is more than an online resume. It is your digital professional identity.

You don't need years of experience to make an impact. Start by showcasing your skills, sharing your knowledge, and continuously learning.

Remember: Don't just create a LinkedIn profile. Build a personal brand that represents who you are and who you aspire to become.

Are We Building Successful Businesses or Sustainable Organizations?

A business can be performing well today and still be inadequately prepared for tomorrow.

Profitability, growth and market share matter. But they tell us more about what an organization is achieving now than how well it is equipped to sustain those achievements.

Consider a business that has enjoyed decades of success. Its leadership knows the market, its customers are loyal, and its operating model has consistently delivered results.

What happens when the conditions that supported that success begin to change?

Experience can be a competitive advantage. It can also reinforce assumptions that deserve to be challenged. Familiar practices may remain unquestioned precisely because they have worked so well.

The risk is not necessarily poor leadership. Sometimes, success itself makes the case for change harder to see.

So perhaps the more demanding question is this:

How much of today’s success are we converting into the capabilities needed for tomorrow?

Are we developing people who can make sound decisions without relying on a few experienced individuals? Are our systems becoming stronger as the business grows? Are we building the capacity to respond when customers, competitors or technology change the rules?

This is not an argument for expansion at any cost, or for replacing what still works. Financial discipline matters. Stability can be a strength.

But there is a difference between protecting a genuine competitive advantage and protecting a familiar way of operating.

Throughout my career, I’ve believed that leadership should leave behind more than a record of results. It should develop people, standards and organizational capabilities that remain valuable beyond any individual’s tenure.

The same principle applies at the enterprise level. Ownership may change. Leaders will move on. Markets will evolve. Continuity depends on more than appointing a successor or preserving an established name.

No organization can guarantee its future. Even well-managed businesses face disruption and difficult choices.

But perhaps we should judge progress through two lenses: the performance we deliver today, and the strength we are building for what comes next.

Because a successful period in a company’s history is not necessarily proof of a business prepared for its future.

#LeadershipReflections #BusinessLeadership #OrganizationalResilience

LEADERSHIP IS ABOUT CHANGING YOUR PERSPECTIVE.

Sometimes, all it takes is a different point of view to see things you couldn’t see before.

Looking out this airplane window got me thinking about manufacturing leadership.

When you’re on the production floor every day, it’s easy to get caught up in the same routines, the same challenges, the same problems, and the same ways of doing things.

But great manufacturing leaders understand something important:

You cannot solve tomorrow’s problems with yesterday’s perspective.

As leaders, we need to learn to look through different lenses.

🔹 The operator’s lens: What challenges are the people doing the actual work facing every day?

🔹 The quality lens: Are we addressing the root cause, or are we simply fixing the symptoms?

🔹 The customer’s lens: Are we delivering what the customer truly needs?

🔹 The financial lens: Where are we losing time, resources, and profitability?

🔹 The leadership lens: Are we developing people, or are we just managing production numbers?

Sometimes, what looks like an employee problem is actually a process problem.

What looks like a performance issue might be a lack of training.

What looks like a production delay might be poor planning, communication, or an inefficient workflow.

And sometimes, the biggest obstacle to improvement is the fact that we’ve always done things a certain way.

I’ve learned that effective manufacturing leadership isn’t about having all the answers.

It’s about asking better questions, listening to different perspectives, challenging assumptions, and having the courage to look at things differently.

Before you change the people, examine the process. Before you point fingers, look in the mirror. Before you make a decision, change your lens.

Because continuous improvement starts with a willingness to see things differently.

A question for fellow manufacturing leaders:

When was the last time you stepped away from your usual perspective and looked at your operation through someone else’s eyes?

Your best employee might be your worst management decision.

Managing people requires an entirely different skill set: communication, delegation, conflict resolution, accountability, and the ability to develop someone else's potential.
And here's something businesses often overlook: Not every high performer wants to manage people.

Before making that promotion, ask whether the employee has the desire and aptitude to lead. And if they do, give them the training and support to succeed.

For business owners looking to grow, his four steps offer a practical roadmap:

1. Discover. Define who your business needs, what success in the role looks like, and why the right person would choose to join you. Clarity starts before the interview.

2. Direct. Turn individual effort into a shared direction. Establish clear goals, meaningful KPIs, and consistent coaching. People need to understand both the destination and their responsibility in getting there.

3. Develop. Make culture visible in everyday decisions: what you recognize, what you tolerate, and how you hold people accountable. Develop the judgment and skills your future leaders will need.

4. Duplicate. Scale by developing leaders who can develop others. Strong individual performance deserves recognition; leadership responsibility requires preparation, judgment, and the ability to help others succeed.

Before adding headcount, examine your processes. Before promoting someone, assess their readiness. Before blaming the team, examine the clarity and support you have provided.

In my experience leading sales teams, ambitious targets become credible when people have clear ownership, coaching, and the authority to execute.

The real test of your leadership is how effectively your team can move the business forward without waiting for you.

How Strong Leadership Teams Turn Year-End Lessons Into Next-Year Advantage 

Two companies are ending the year with similar financial results.

Both experienced revenue growth, unexpected challenges, missed opportunities, and some decisions that did not deliver the expected outcomes.
One leadership team reviews the numbers, explains the variances, and moves on to setting new targets.

The other asks a different question:
“What have we learned this year that can help us make better decisions next year?”
That single question can make all the difference.
The strongest leadership teams don't just review performance. They turn experience into strategic advantage.

As we prepare for the coming year, here are five things effective leadership teams should prioritize:
🔹 Turn Mistakes into Strategic Lessons: Understand what went wrong, why it happened, and what must change to prevent a recurrence.
🔹 Identify What Created Real Value: Look beyond revenue growth to profitability, cash flow, operational efficiency, and returns on investment.
🔹 Challenge Existing Assumptions: Just because a strategy worked in the past does not mean it will remain effective in a changing business environment.
🔹 Align Leadership Priorities: Ensure the CEO, CFO, and other executives share a clear understanding of the organization's financial realities, strategic direction, and resource requirements.
🔹 Translate Lessons into Action: Convert insights into measurable priorities, stronger processes, better investment decisions, and clear accountability.

The difference between an average leadership team and a high-performing one is not that one makes mistakes while the other does not.
It is how quickly they learn, adapt, and turn those lessons into better decisions.

Year-end should not simply mark the completion of another business cycle. It should provide the intelligence needed to enter the next one with greater clarity, stronger capabilities, and better strategic focus.

As leaders, we must remember that experience alone does not create competitive advantage. What we do with that experience does.

The real question is:
Are we carrying forward the lessons of this year, or are we preparing to repeat the same mistakes with bigger targets?

Part 2: How to Stop Being the Bottleneck

Want your leadership team to make more decisions without you? Stop being the answer to every question.

In my last post, I talked about how business owners can unintentionally become the bottleneck in their own companies.So how do you fix it?

Start with something simple.
Look at the last five decisions that landed on your desk. For each one, ask yourself:
- Did this decision really require my involvement?
- Does my leader know they have the authority to make this decision?
- Do they have the information and skills needed to make a good decision?
- Am I comfortable letting them make a decision differently than I would?

That last question is a big one. Because developing leaders means accepting that they won’t always do things exactly the way you would.

And that’s OK.

Your job as CEO isn’t to make every decision. It’s to build a team capable of making good decisions without you. That requires clear expectations, trust, accountability, and sometimes letting people learn from mistakes.

Because, if your business can’t make decisions without you, how much can it really grow?

One of the biggest mistakes we make in leadership is confusing confidence with having all the answers.

I’ve sat in enough rooms to know that experience doesn’t make us immune to bad decisions. And a fancy title certainly doesn’t make every idea a good one.

The leaders I respect most aren’t the ones who always get it right. They’re the ones who create space for honest conversations, listen when challenged, and care more about getting results than protecting their egos.

Because the moment protecting your reputation becomes more important than doing what’s right, you’ve lost sight of who you’re supposed to be leading.

That’s a conversation worth having.

What’s one leadership lesson that changed the way you lead?

#Leadership #ExecutiveLeadership #Accountability #LeadershipDevelopment

THE TWO-EARS, ONE-MOUTH LEADERSHIP TEST

We've all heard the old saying:

"We have two ears and one mouth. We should use them in that proportion."

But how often do leaders actually follow that advice?

Especially when delivering corrective feedback!

Think about your last difficult conversation with an employee.

Who did most of the talking?

Did you ask questions and genuinely listen to the answers?

Or did you spend most of the conversation explaining what went wrong, why it was unacceptable, and what needed to change?

Here's the problem:

When leaders do all the talking, they may miss the very information they need to solve the problem.

Perhaps the employee misunderstood the assignment.

Perhaps expectations weren't clear.

Perhaps they lacked the necessary resources, training, or confidence.

Or perhaps there's something happening that you simply don't know about.

You won't discover any of that if you're too busy delivering a lecture!

During my years coaching NCAA Division I athletes, I learned that understanding WHY someone was struggling was often just as important as identifying WHAT they were doing wrong.

The same principle applies in business.

Before prescribing a solution, try asking:

• "Walk me through what happened."

• "What challenges were you facing?"

• "Is there something I'm missing?"

• "What do you think would help us improve the situation?"

And then comes the difficult part...

STOP TALKING. START LISTENING.

Listening doesn't mean avoiding accountability or accepting excuses.

It means gathering the information necessary to make better coaching decisions.

Sometimes, the employee's explanation will change your understanding of the situation.

Other times, it will simply confirm that corrective action is needed.

Either way, you'll be better prepared to lead.

Great coaches don't just deliver feedback. They create conversations that lead to improvement.

In my latest article, Stop Criticizing. Start Coaching, I share practical strategies for turning difficult feedback conversations into opportunities for growth, accountability, and stronger performance.

You can be excellent at DSA and still struggle during your first year as a software engineer. And that's completely normal. 🫣 
Because technical interviews and real-world engineering evaluate different dimensions of your abilities.

In interviews, you're often expected to solve a well-defined problem within a limited time.

At work, the problem itself might not be clear.

You need to understand existing systems, question assumptions, communicate decisions, handle unexpected failures and think about the engineers who will maintain your code.

Here are 5 skills I'd focus on beyond DSA:

1. Writing: Explain technical decisions clearly. Good documentation reduces unnecessary back-and-forth.

2. Ownership: Don't stop at completing a ticket. Understand whether the underlying problem is actually solved.

3. Debugging: Investigate root causes instead of repeatedly fixing symptoms.

4. Simplicity: Write code that another engineer can understand and maintain.

5. Communication: Share context, raise concerns early, and explain trade-offs instead of simply presenting solutions.

None of these replaces technical fundamentals.
They complement them.

Being able to write code gets you started. 
Being able to take responsibility for what you build sets you apart.

If I Were Starting Out as a Software Developer Today, Would I Still Go to University?

It’s an interesting question.

For years, the traditional pathway into software development has been pretty straightforward. Study computer science or software engineering, learn to code, understand architecture, databases and systems, and build your experience from there.

But AI is changing that.

We’re already seeing developers using AI agents to write code, build applications, troubleshoot problems and accelerate delivery.

And that’s only going to improve.

So where does that leave someone who’s about to spend three or four years studying software development?

Will the skills they’re learning today still be relevant when they graduate?

Or will the real value shift towards understanding business problems, designing solutions, managing AI agents and knowing whether the software being produced is actually fit for purpose?

I don’t believe software engineering knowledge suddenly becomes irrelevant. Quite the opposite. Someone still needs to understand architecture, security, scalability and what happens when things go wrong.

But here’s what I’m wondering.

If AI increasingly handles the coding, how does the next generation develop the deep technical understanding that experienced engineers have spent years acquiring?

And are our universities adapting quickly enough to prepare students for that reality?

If you were 18 today and considering a career in software development, would you still take the traditional university route?

Or would you approach it differently?

I’d be interested in hearing from software engineers, technology leaders and particularly those involved in educating our next generation of developers.

I strongly believe that one of the best ways to level up as a software engineer is to write lots of code, especially early in your career. 

I've *handcoded* many projects in the past, spanning across various languages. Games, websites, CLI tools, SSG frameworks, you name it.

But times have changed, both ceiling and floor have been raised.

Here are some projects I recommend undergrads / junior software engineers to build to learn + stay relevant:

- Personal portfolio website w/ blog using a static site generator
- Multi-page marketing website
- Small web/mobile games
- Reader clients (e.g. hacker news client)

Then progress to full stack apps / systems:

- CRUD apps (kanban, personal library)
- Small social network for your family / friends
- Build a design system (use a headless library like Base UI and Tailwind CSS)
- AI chat app like ChatGPT
- Prompt playground to save prompts and test different model providers
- Unsplash clone that tags each image and allow semantic search
- Personal notetaking app with RAG search

Lastly, build some advanced apps:

- Generative media AI apps
- Desktop coding agents
- Real-time chat application
- Drawing / Canvas / whiteboard apps
- Email client
- Multiplayer games
- Web crawler with semantic search

Pick a project that either solves a problem for yourself/others, or you can learn how something works under the hood.

To level up your software engineering skills, code for fun, and not just for work.

Cover the core logic, not every getter.

Most engineering career frameworks are written by HR. They rely on vague phrases like "demonstrates domain mastery" or "drives cross-functional alignment."
 
Strip away the corporate buzzwords, and real technical progression comes down to two things: how novel the problems are, and who originated the work.
 
Junior Engineer: Foundation & Execution Focuses on learning the codebase, tools, and team processes. Takes well-defined tickets and delivers clean code within established patterns.
 
Senior Engineer: Autonomous Execution Takes an ambiguous problem, designs the schema or system boundary, and drives it to production without hand-holding. Executes known patterns reliably.
 
Tech Lead: Invention & Novel Problem-Solving Solves problems that haven't been solved in the building yet. Creates the new patterns, authors defensible IP, and builds the core architecture the rest of the team relies on.
 
Staff Engineer: Internal Entrepreneurship Doesn't wait for a roadmap ticket. Spots an architectural bottleneck, a cloud cost sink, or a structural reliability risk on their own, designs the fix, and moves the company's financial needle.
 
Juniors learn the patterns. Seniors execute the patterns. Tech Leads invent the patterns. Staff Engineers invent the work.
 
If you're paying Staff salaries to people waiting on Jira tickets, you don't have a talent problem—you have a role definition problem.
 
How does your organization distinguish between a Tech Lead and a Staff Engineer?

How naïve I was 20 years ago, thinking software architect is a technical role! It is primarily about education and politics of influence. And on the third side (there's always a third side) it's the good old ego / power struggle - part of the human nature. And your job as an Architect is to make difference working within this mandala. It requires ironclad resolve and unbending power of will, combined with a certain mythical Gandalf façade to soften the otherwise harsh message. Education and influence IS the job.

text:
Want to raise your first $500,000?
Here is something most first-time founders get wrong.
They start pitching investors before they even know what investors want.
That can cost them months of wasted meetings.

I have raised funding for my own startups, and one thing I have learned is that fundraising becomes much easier when you understand what investors expect.
So here is what I would do if I were raising my first pre-seed round today.
Before asking anyone for money, I would book five meetings with seed-stage investors.
Not to pitch them.
Not to ask for a check.
But to understand what would make my startup attractive for their next investment round.

I would ask one question:
"What would you need to see from my startup in the next 12 months to seriously consider investing?"
Then I would listen.

Maybe they want $20,000 in monthly recurring revenue.
Maybe they want 100 paying customers or strong customer retention.
Now you have something most founders do not.
A fundraising roadmap informed by real investor feedback.
When you approach pre-seed investors, you can explain exactly what milestones their money will help you achieve.

Do not start fundraising by asking for money.
Start by understanding what makes your startup investable.

text:
Answer the Question the Investor Actually Asked

Founders sometimes answer an investor’s question without addressing it. Ask, “How do you know customers will pay?” and you may hear about the product, market size, or enthusiastic demos. Those points may be encouraging, but they are not payment evidence.
Investors want specifics: pricing discussions, paid pilots, contract conversions, renewals, and expansions. If asked about customer concentration, growing pipeline does not remove the risk. If asked about gross margin, revenue growth does not explain the economics. If asked why you are raising $3 million, market size does not show what the capital will accomplish.

When “I Don’t Know” Is the Better Investor Answer

A founder once told me, “I always need to have an answer in an investor meeting.” I understood the instinct, but not the rule.

* You should know your revenue, burn, runway, customers, pipeline, financing terms, and what the new capital will accomplish.
But some numbers won’t be in front of you, and some analysis won’t be done yet. That is not automatically a problem. Guessing is.

If you say gross margin is 72% and the data room later shows 61%, the conversation shifts to why the number changed. I would rather hear: “I don’t have the exact number, and I don’t want to guess. Let me confirm it and follow up.” That shows judgment, not a lack of preparation.

Know what you should know. Admit what you need to verify. Then close the gap. Credibility comes from having the answer and not inventing one, if you do not.

text:
Every founder gets the same advice:
 
“Get a warm intro.”
 
Here’s what nobody says out loud.
 
If you don’t already know investors, you can’t get a warm intro to investors.
 
Think about that.
 
You built a real business. Customers. Revenue. A team.
And the advice is to go find someone who knows someone who might forward your email.
 
So founders do the only thing left.
They pay someone who claims to know investors.
 
$20K upfront. A success fee. Sometimes equity.
 
Who the f*** designed this system?!
 
I’ve sat on the investor side of the table too. Here’s what founders don’t see:
 
Investors aren’t hiding.
They’re buried in pre-revenue decks and broker pitches, looking for companies with real revenue.
 
Founders looking for investors.
Investors looking for founders.
And a middleman charging a toll in between.
 
A warm intro isn’t a strategy.
It’s a gatekeeper.
 
If you’re doing real revenue, you shouldn’t need permission to meet an investor.
 
Founders: how did you land your first investor meeting? Warm intro, cold email, or something else? 👇
 
#Fundraising #Founders #VentureCapital #StartupFunding #Entrepreneurship

Fundraising Readiness · Day 19/90

Rehearse the questions investors will ask before they ask them.

Write down your answers to these five, out loud, in under 30 seconds each:
1. Why you, and why now?
2. Who pays you today, and why?
3. What happens if a bigger player copies you?

Investors don't ignore every startup. Sometimes, founders are simply approaching the wrong investors.
One mistake I often see in fundraising is founders sending the same pitch deck and email to hundreds of investors, hoping someone will respond.
But fundraising isn't just about reaching out. It's about reaching out to the right people.
Before approaching an investor, do your homework:
→ Investment thesis: Do they invest in your industry, business model and stage?
→ Cheque size: Does your fundraising requirement align with their typical ticket size?
→ Portfolio: What companies have they already invested in? Are there any synergies or conflicts?
→ Recent investments: How actively have they been investing this year?
→ Fund availability: Do they still have capital to deploy, or have they already allocated most of their current fund?
→ Investment background: Understand their previous investments, preferred sectors and what they look for in founders.
Why does this matter?
Imagine approaching a pre-seed startup investor when you're raising Series A, or pitching a healthcare startup to an investor focused entirely on SaaS.
Even a great pitch can go nowhere.
Fundraising is not a numbers game. It's a relevance game.
Instead of sending 100 random emails, spend time identifying 10 relevant investors and understanding why your startup fits their thesis.
A little research before outreach can save weeks of follow-ups and create much better conversations.

text:
88% of VC-backed founders walk away with $0.

Not because 88% of startups are necessarily worthless.

A new study by researchers from Wharton and the University of Zurich analysed 157,669 startups and 248,454 founders between 1987 and 2025.

The findings are striking:

→ 88% of founders received no exit proceeds.

→ The top 1% captured 79% of total founder exit value.

→ Even a successful company exit doesn’t guarantee a successful outcome for its founders.

Having built companies, raised hundreds of millions and invested in over 100 startups, I’ve learned one important lesson:

The valuation you raise at matters. But the terms you sign can matter even more.

Liquidation preferences. Anti-dilution clauses. Option pools. Founder vesting. Successive funding rounds.

These can make the difference between building a valuable company and actually capturing some of that value.

Of course, many founders receive nothing simply because their companies fail. But others discover too late that a successful exit doesn’t necessarily mean a payday.

My advice to founders:

Don’t just model your next fundraising round. Model your exit waterfall.

Understand exactly what you would take home if your company sold for €10M, €50M or €100M.

And remember: raising more capital isn’t always winning.

Sometimes, retaining ownership, building a profitable business and keeping control is the better outcome.

At Enduring Founder, I share practical fundraising tools, including dilution modelling and guides to understanding term sheets before signing.

https://lnkd.in/eaVMKCcx

Build yourself to build what lasts.

Financial Management Is About More Than Making Money. It's About Making Money Work for You.
One of the most important lessons I've learned in business is that generating income and managing wealth are two very different skills.
Financial success isn't simply measured by how much money you earn. It's also about how effectively you allocate resources, manage cash flow, prepare for uncertainty, and make decisions with a long-term perspective.
I believe a sound financial management strategy should focus on four key principles:
Cash Flow Management: Maintain sufficient liquidity to meet obligations and take advantage of opportunities.
Strategic Allocation: Diversify resources according to financial goals, risk tolerance, and time horizons.
Risk Management: Understand potential exposure before making significant financial commitments.
Long-Term Planning: Build sustainable financial structures rather than chasing short-term gains.
Markets will change, business conditions will evolve, and unexpected challenges will arise. A well-structured financial plan helps create stability and provides greater flexibility when circumstances change.
Ultimately, wealth management isn't about making every decision perfectly. It's about making informed decisions consistently.
Build a financial foundation that supports the life and future you want to create.

After years of leading digital transformation in Finance at Roche, one lesson continues to stand out: it's always been about people.

AI is accelerating what's possible, but the fundamentals haven't changed: business problems first, data second, and technology last. The real opportunity is empowering people to think differently, make better decisions, and turn innovation into meaningful impact.

I recently had the privilege of co-leading the “Digital Finance in Practice” course for the Master in International Financial Management students at Lucerne University of Applied Sciences and Arts, alongside my colleague Anahita Rippstein.

Bringing our experiences from Roche into the classroom was incredibly rewarding. I was particularly impressed by the students' curiosity, fresh perspectives, and willingness to challenge assumptions as they worked through real-world Finance challenges and CFO-level trade-offs.

It reinforced something I see in my own work every day: the future of Finance isn't simply about what AI and data can do, but what people are empowered to do with them. That takes curiosity, sound judgment, collaboration, and the courage to challenge the status quo. And in healthcare, it means keeping patients at the heart of the decisions we make.

A big thank you to Marielle Beyer, Svenja Amrhein, and Sandra Keller for sharing their perspectives as guest speakers, to Anahita Rippstein for being a fantastic teaching partner, and to Professor Imke Keimer for making this experience possible.

My takeaway for the next generation of Finance leaders: Don't just learn to use the technology. Learn to ask better questions, challenge conventional thinking, and connect the numbers to what truly matters.

That's how we shape the Future of Finance.

Finance Fundamentals: Understanding the Different Types of Banking

Banking is one of the most important parts of the financial system. However, not all banks perform the same functions.

Here are four major types of banking:

1. Retail Banking
Provides financial services to individuals, including savings accounts, personal loans and debit cards.

2. Commercial Banking
Works with businesses by providing business loans, managing cash flow and supporting financial operations.

3. Investment Banking
Helps companies raise capital, manage mergers and acquisitions, and conduct major financial transactions.

4. Central Banking
Oversees monetary policy, manages interest rates and contributes to financial stability.

I believe understanding these fundamentals is an important starting point for developing knowledge of the basic finance.

Come to think of it, are today's Core banking Applications really supporting growth?

Banks have invested heavily in technology. Core banking, lending, payments, CRM, digital channels, reporting, compliance systems and countless integrations.

Yet, introducing a new product or improving an existing process can still take months, involve multiple vendors and require several technology teams.

How did we get here?

Over time, financial institutions have accumulated applications to solve individual business problems. Each application may serve a purpose, but together they can create a complex technology environment that becomes increasingly difficult and expensive to manage.

The bigger question is no longer simply which application a bank should acquire next.

It is whether banks are becoming too dependent on the applications they have already acquired.

Imagine being able to introduce new banking capabilities without necessarily adding another standalone application.

Imagine intelligent agents coordinating activities across existing systems — supporting lending, collections, reporting, customer service and compliance — while the bank retains control of its financial infrastructure, policies and approvals.

This is one of the ideas driving the emergence of AI Agent Banking.

In Edition 02 of my newsletter, Future of Banking: Agentic Era, 
I explore:
Why application dependency is becoming a strategic challenge for banks.
How technology maintenance can consume resources meant for innovation.

Why integrating existing systems is often harder than buying new ones.
Whether replacing the core banking system is always the answer.
How AI agents could help institutions get more value from their existing technology investments.

I believe the future competitive advantage may not belong to the bank with the most software applications.

It may belong to the bank that gets the most intelligence and business value from the technology it already has.

Unpopular opinion: Africa doesn’t have a shortage of fintech founders. It has a shortage of founders paying attention to ordinary problems. In 2024, fintech took about 60% of African tech equity funding. It fell to roughly 32% in 2025, but our reflex is still the same. A farmer can’t get inputs, so we build a lending app. A school struggles with attendance, so we build a payment app. We keep mistaking “a fintech product exists” for “a financial problem exists.”

The most instructive company I studied this month is a school bus app out of Georgetown, Texas. It has no lending, no crypto and no cross-border payments. It sells to school districts, and it solves one question every parent asks: did my child get home safely? 

Founders, stop building what’s fashionable at pitch competitions. Investors, the next indispensable African technology company may be in the sector nobody wanted to discuss at your last demo day. 

Disagree?

In 2015, Nik Storonsky was pitching Revolut to raise £1.5 million.

Zero revenue.

What started as an ambitious fintech startup became one of the world’s most valuable private technology companies.

1️⃣ Sell the vision, not your limitations
Investors need to understand how big your company can become, not just where it stands today.

Storonsky wasn’t apologizing for being early. He was communicating why traditional banking was ready for disruption.

A compelling pitch opens doors, but building a great business is what ultimately creates lasting value.

Every billion-dollar company was once an early-stage startup.

Limited resources. Uncertain outcomes. A vision that few people believed in.

The best founders don’t just pitch what they’ve built.

Clara Raises $105 Million: The Race to Reinvent Corporate Finance in Latin America

The future of fintech may not be built around consumer payments alone. Increasingly, investors are backing platforms that help businesses manage the complexity of money itself.

Clara, a five-year-old São Paulo-based fintech startup, has secured $105 million in fresh financing to expand its corporate financial management business.

The funding comprises a $65 million Series C round anchored by Citius, Kaszek Ventures, and DEG, alongside $40 million in renewed growth financing from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund.

Clara helps businesses manage corporate spending, invoices, bills, and cross-border payments through an integrated financial platform.

The problem it is addressing is significant. Businesses operating across Latin America often navigate fragmented payment systems, complex financial administration, and cross-border transaction challenges.

Clara's proposition is to bring these financial operations together, giving companies greater visibility and control over their spending.

But the bigger story is the growing confidence of investors in Latin America's fintech infrastructure.

While much of the global AI and technology conversation focuses on consumer-facing applications, companies like Clara are targeting the operational foundations of business: payments, financial visibility, expense management, and cash-flow efficiency.

For emerging markets, this development carries an important lesson.

The next generation of valuable fintech companies may not simply be those helping people move money. They may be the companies rebuilding how businesses manage, monitor, and deploy capital.

The future of fintech belongs to platforms that solve real financial infrastructure problems, not just those that make transactions faster.

Is fintech funding making a comeback?

After a challenging few years for investment markets, the latest numbers suggest confidence is returning to the sector.

It's where that capital is flowing.

Large investors appear to be backing fewer, bigger opportunities, signalling renewed confidence in fintech businesses that have proven scale, strong economics and a clear path to growth. 

For founders, this creates both an opportunity and a challenge:
✅ More capital is available for the right businesses
✅ Investor confidence is recovering
❌ Competition for larger rounds remains intense
❌ Expectations around profitability and execution are higher than ever

The bigger question for the industry is whether this marks the start of a sustained recovery or simply reflects investor appetite for a small number of standout fintechs.

As we head into 2027, it'll be fascinating to see whether funding strength broadens across the ecosystem or remains concentrated in the largest deals.

Are we witnessing the return of fintech's growth cycle, or is investment becoming increasingly focused on a handful of market leaders?

The most important number in modern macroeconomics is unexplained.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics went to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for the microfoundations of macroeconomic stabilisation. Embedded in that work is a finding every central bank now models: roughly 80% of households behave as forward-looking consumers. The other 20% live hand-to-mouth.

Nobel-anchored. Estimable. Stable across countries. But taken as a brute fact — never explained.

Our new working paper asks the prior question: what makes a household hand-to-mouth?
Not income. Two households at identical income differ in what they can feasibly do — health, housing burden, credit access, mobility — before any decision is made. Our claim: the 80/20 split is a measurable signature of underlying capability heterogeneity. And because it varies across countries and time, its covariates can be estimated. Capability becomes a variable, not a metaphor.

Why it matters:

▪ The same shock doesn't act on a representative agent — it acts on a distribution of capacities to adjust.
▪ Your workforce sits in that distribution — participation, absenteeism, benefit exposure.
▪ Capability gets priced as a reduction in future liabilities — the bridge between capability and capital.

The mechanism is set out in our SSRN paper The Household Affordability Frontier: structural costs form a threshold beyond which households optimise for survival rather than invest in capability — the frontier we argue produces the split itself.

An extension claim, not a rival claim. We accept the microfoundations revolution in full — and ask what produces the deciders.

text:
التحليل الجزئي والكلي 📊
Micro-economic Analysis & Macro-economic Analysis

يُعرف التحليل الاقتصادي بأنه أسلوب علمي يتعرف به على العوامل المؤثرة في الظواهر والمسائل الاقتصادية، ويفسّر أسبابها، ويستخلص منه النظريات والقوانين الاقتصادية.

وينقسم إلى قسمين متكاملين:
🔹 التحليل الجزئي (Micro-economic Analysis): يدرس الوحدات الاقتصادية الفردية، كالمستهلك والمنشأة والسوق، وقضايا تشكيل أسعار السلع والخدمات.
🔹 التحليل الكلي (Macro-economic Analysis): يدرس الاقتصاد الوطني ككل، ومنه الدخل القومي والبطالة والتضخم والاستثمار.

وهذا يقودنا إلى مغالطة مهمة: ما يصح على الفرد لا يصح بالضرورة على المجتمع. فالادخار الفردي مفيد، لكن إذا ادّخر الجميع وتوقف الإنفاق، انخفض الطلب الكلي، ثم الإنتاج والدخل القومي.

📘 المصطلحات:
Micro-economic Analysis = التحليل الجزئي
Macro-economic Analysis = التحليل الكلي
Fallacy of Composition = مغالطة التركيب

🔊 النطق: «ميكرو إيكونوميك أناليسيس» · «ماكرو إيكونوميك أناليسيس» · «فالاسي أوف كومبوزيشن»

─────────────

Micro-economic and Macro-economic Analysis 📊

Economic analysis is a scientific method for identifying the factors that influence economic phenomena and problems, explaining their causes, and deriving theories and laws from them.

It divides into two complementary parts:
🔹 Micro-economic Analysis: studies individual economic units such as the consumer, the firm and the market, and how prices of goods and services are formed.
🔹 Macro-economic Analysis: studies the national economy as a whole, including national income, unemployment, inflation and investment.

This leads to an important fallacy: what holds for the individual does not necessarily hold for society. Individual saving is useful, but if everyone saves and spending stops, total demand falls, then production and national income.

📘 Key terms:
Micro-economic Analysis = التحليل الجزئي
