A successful AI pilot is one thing. Scaling it across multiple warehouses is another.
 
In Part 3 of our Intelligent Automation in Warehousing: An AI Roadmap series, we're looking at scale, and our research reveals an interesting disconnect.
 
42% of integration partners say existing systems aren't ready to support more AI, compared to just 19% of customers.
 
Why the gap?
 
Customers experience AI through the interface. Partners see the complexity behind the integrations.
 
And that's where many scaling challenges begin.
 
The organizations getting this right aren't rebuilding their AI solutions for every new site. They're investing in unified data, standardized APIs, repeatable processes and measurable results.
 
Because scaling AI isn't just about the technology but about building the infrastructure that makes growth possible.
 
Next in the series: Adoption. Why deploying AI doesn't necessarily mean people will use it.

A polished AI demo answers one question:

Can the model do something impressive?

It does not answer the question that matters on a difficult operating day:

Can our company run, govern, and recover this system?

Before choosing an AI implementation partner, ask them to put four artifacts on the table:

• A process map that includes the exceptions, not only the happy path
• A decision-rights matrix showing what the AI may do and where a person remains accountable
• An evaluation and recovery plan covering bad data, unavailable systems, incorrect outputs, and unauthorized actions
• A handover package with runbooks, administrative access, change control, training, and clear internal owners

If those artifacts do not exist, you are still evaluating a promise—not an operating capability.

A credible implementation partner should leave behind more than working software. They should leave a process your organization can understand, govern, operate, recover, and improve.

The question I would ask before signing is simple:

What will our team be able to operate after you leave?

The integration of artificial intelligence into lean operating business units gives employees the capacity to digest more, action more efficiently, and enables them to build reports or tools that uniquely set them individually up for success. On the flip side, it also puts them on the bleeding edge of trouble shooting technical issues, data validation, and deployment issues when sharing those tools. 

Plugins give your desktop AI the ability to automatically review coding, correct, and test tools for you. 

Skills can be used to prevent repetitive issues in the future and guide your AI through a repeatable workflow. 

Coupling these two together with a strong sense of creativity and knowledge of your workplace's data landscape, will make you unstoppable.

Too many AI initiatives remain stuck in pilot mode in renewable energy.  The biggest setback often comes from selecting too many use cases, not too few. 

In fact, organizations can typically achieve 60% to 70% of their AI value potential through just 10 to 15 use cases. 

In week one, if you cannot clearly state which KPIs you will be measuring and explain the mechanism for financial impact, you are not running an AI initiative. You are conducting research. Move on to the next use case.  

Drawing on our experience supporting AI transformations, we outline six lessons to help firms identify and prioritize AI initiatives with a focus on value creation from the outset, solving operational constraints, moving fast with disciplined governance, and having the right processes and people in place to scale.  

For leaders looking to accelerate AI adoption while maintaining a strong focus on measurable impact, this is a practical roadmap to do exactly that.

Ten years ago, I placed a bet on AI.

I was exploring two emerging technologies: artificial intelligence, particularly machine learning and computer vision, and blockchain.

Both intrigued me. 

But I could see a clearer path for AI to solve problems that affected people’s everyday lives. That’s where I chose to focus. 

Spent couple of months self-learning on Coursera and Udacity and 

That decision shaped the next decade of my career.

I’ve since worked on AI implementations across healthcare , transportation, financial services, and the public sector.

Along the way, my CTO diaries have filled up with lessons about what it takes to make AI useful:

1. Start with the use case.
Name the problem, the person experiencing it, and the decision you want to improve before choosing the technology.

2. Build responsibility into the design.
Privacy, governance, testing, and oversight need to shape development from the beginning.

3. Make explanations useful.
People need to understand why a system flagged something and what evidence supports it, especially when a decision may face scrutiny in court.

3. Treat data readiness as foundational.
Access, quality, context, and permissions determine what a solution can reliably do.

4. Design around the actual workflow.
Spend time with the people doing the work. Their constraints should shape the solution.

5. Give human reviewer a clear purpose.
Define who examines an output, what they need to verify, and who has authority to act.
Measure outcomes.

6. Establish a baseline. Track whether AI improves review time, decision quality, or service delivery.

7. Test beyond the demo.

Real implementation includes exceptions, incomplete data, integration, monitoring, and someone accountable for keeping it working.

These lessons have shaped a product I’m proud to introduce through The AI Blueprint: iPrism.

 💡 iPrism helps investigators prioritize unusual financial transactions for review and understand why they were flagged.  💡 

It brings together anomaly detection and explainable indicators so an investigator can examine the reasons, consider the context, and decide what warrants further investigation.

A flag is a starting point. The investigator reviews the evidence and approves any next steps.

Ten years ago, I chose AI because I could see its potential to help people.

With iPrism, I’m putting those years of learning into a product built around the person making the decision.

Not Every AI Use Case Deserves a Budget. Here's How to Decide.
AI is exciting. But excitement doesn't equal business value. One of the biggest mistakes organizations make is investing in AI solutions before determining whether they're solving the right problem. Just because AI can do something doesn't mean your business should invest in it. Before approving your next AI initiative, ask a few questions: 

🎯 1. Business Value: What measurable problem are we solving? Will this reduce costs, increase revenue, or improve customer experience?
⚙️ 2. Implementation Effort: How difficult will this be to implement and integrate into existing workflows?
📊 3. Data Readiness: Do we have the quality, accessible data needed to make this successful?
🛡️ 4. Risk & Governance: What are the security, compliance, and operational risks?
⏱️ 5. Time to Value: How quickly can we demonstrate meaningful results?

Here's a practical example: A customer service team is considering two AI initiatives:
Option A: An AI chatbot that handles routine customer inquiries.
Option B: An AI-powered analytics solution that predicts customer churn.

Both have potential. But which one should receive funding first? The answer depends on business priorities, implementation readiness, expected ROI, and risk—not which technology sounds more impressive.

💡 My takeaway: The best AI strategy doesn't start with selecting tools. It starts with identifying and prioritizing the right business opportunities.

What matters most when your organization evaluates an AI investment: ROI, speed, or strategic impact?

The founder who publishes, who shows their thinking, who lets the right people see what they are building before a formal raise — that founder has warmed the room before they ever walked into it.

The founder who builds in silence and then sends cold decks into the void is asking investors to make a cold decision about a stranger.

Your idea does not sell itself. Your story does. And your story cannot travel if it lives only in your head and a pitch deck nobody has seen.

$120 million in funding. A promising idea. An innovative product.

And ultimately, a failed business.

What went wrong?

In this excerpt from today's Pinnacle Process Group Basecamp Workshop, I share the story of Juicero and an important lesson for entrepreneurs.

Support is not validation.

You can have enthusiastic investors, encouraging friends and family, and a product that everyone agrees sounds like a great idea.

But there's a fundamental difference between people believing in your business and customers demonstrating that they need what you're offering.

Funding provides resources.

Encouragement provides motivation.

Validation provides evidence.

And without that evidence, even $120 million might not be enough.

Before asking how to fund your idea, consider whether you've done enough to validate it.

Are you building something people admire, or something customers actually need?

Turning down $2M in term sheets was not the update I was expecting since I last had Jay on the podcast in June 2025. 

But fyeah Jay! Huge respect for that.

It takes a lot of foresight to do that, and there are so many good lessons from that decision.

Jay Kriner is a serial entrepreneur and dad. His first company, a belt buckle beer opener, landed him on Shark Tank. Now he’s the founder and CEO of Gale Project Technologies, which also recently announced is going to the moon. Literally!

Here are a few highlights of Jay’s advice from his past year of raising. 

Click to read the full newsletter for more. And be sure to follow Jay K. here on LinkedIn. 🚀 

1. Nothing happens fast, so work backward. If you’re building something to sell, decide what you want to achieve by a certain date. Then figure out how many customers, how much manufacturing, and how much time it’ll take to get there.

2. Ask anyone who’s had any success how they got there. Even a store manager has something to teach you. Collect the pieces of advice. It costs nothing.

3. Look after yourself. Fundraising and building a company take a toll on your health and your family. Keep exercising, and keep an ongoing conversation going with the people closest to you.

How AI Is Shaping the Next Wave of Innovation
Artificial intelligence is moving beyond experimentation and becoming an important part of everyday business operations.
From improving productivity to accelerating product development, AI is helping organizations approach complex challenges in new ways.
What interests me most is not just the technology itself, but how businesses are learning to integrate it into their existing systems and workflows.

Integrating artificial intelligence into mobile applications changes how software interacts with users, yet poor architecture often ruins the experience. Many teams try to run heavy models directly on mobile devices without optimizing memory and battery consumption. When an app heats up or lags during inference, users uninstall it immediately.

I treat AI integration as a core architectural challenge rather than an afterthought. We design hybrid pipelines that balance fast on device processing with scalable cloud computing. By using lightweight models and edge optimization, we keep response times low even on standard hardware. In enterprise mobile apps, this approach enables real time personalization, voice recognition, and visual data analysis without network delays. AI also accelerates our internal development workflow by automating repetitive code generation and regression testing. Instead of spending months on basic setup, our engineers focus on security, data privacy, and smooth user interfaces. Reliable mobile AI requires strict control over data flows and continuous performance monitoring after release. The goal is to deliver intelligent features that feel native and effortless on any screen.

AI innovation is increasingly constrained by how quickly systems can move data, not just how fast they can compute. This shift is driving new approaches to processor architecture, memory design, and hardware-software co-optimization. Have you ever wondered why some salespeople build long-term relationships with customers while others focus only on closing deals?

🔹 2. Listen More, Talk Less

🔹 3. Recommend the Right Solution
Show customers how your product or service can solve their problems and create real value.

UNDERSTANDING SALES MANAGEMENT: WHAT EVERY BUSINESS OWNER SHOULD KNOW

Have you ever wondered why some businesses consistently make sales while others struggle to attract customers, even when they sell similar products?

One important factor behind successful selling is Sales Management.

What is Sales Management?

Sales management involves planning, organising, directing and controlling the activities of a sales force to help an organisation achieve its sales, profit and growth objectives.

In simpler terms, sales management is the process of managing the people, activities, resources and customer relationships involved in selling a company's products or services.

What are the objectives of Sales Management?

There are several objectives, but let's look at four important ones:

1. Achieving Sales Volume

One major objective is to ensure that the organisation meets its sales targets and sells the expected quantity of products or services.

2. Promoting Business Growth

Sales management helps an organisation expand its market share, reach new customers and strengthen its position in the marketplace.

3. Generating Customers

It helps businesses identify potential customers (prospects) and convert them into actual buyers through effective selling strategies.

4. Reducing Sales Costs and Improving Performance

Effective sales management helps organisations use their resources efficiently, minimise unnecessary selling expenses and improve the productivity of their sales team.

A Practical Example:

Imagine a phone and laptop business in Port Harcourt.

The business owner sets monthly sales targets, assigns responsibilities to sales representatives, monitors their performance and develops strategies to attract more customers.

All these activities are part of sales management.

Final Thought:

Selling a product is important, but managing the entire selling process is what helps a business achieve sustainable growth.

What do you think is more important to a business: attracting new customers or retaining existing customers?

How bold is Bank Leumi's CEO move of speaking to us straight from social media? 🏦

On Tuesday (17.11) on Channel 10's Macro panel we discussed it. On one hand, there's real innovation: a CEO communicating company performance directly to the public, not only through a board report. On the other, you have to read between the lines.

The dividend reaches shareholders, which is all of us through investment portfolios and pension funds. But who doesn't benefit? The bank's customers. In a market without real competition, the credit choke on small and mid-sized businesses and on mortgages is felt in each of our pockets. The high profits come out of our pockets, and that isn't talked about enough.

And in Hanan Friedman's scripted video, where every word was written in advance (which is legitimate), the real question goes unaddressed: why are profits so high? They didn't come from excellent banking, but from credit margins. And who's on those platforms? Young people. To me this is more a customer-acquisition marketing move than real accountability to the public.

What do you think? Bold move or marketing platform?

Eight stories highlight the challenges facing banking and fintech as digital finance accelerates, cybercriminals become more sophisticated and established institutions face growing pressure.

Meanwhile, Metro Bank has reportedly put itself up for sale, highlighting the continuing pressure on challenger banks to demonstrate sustainable business models.

🔗 Tokenisation brings risks as well as rewards. As financial markets embrace tokenised assets, the Financial Times warns against overlooking the dangers. Greater efficiency, liquidity and programmability are attractive, but operational resilience, market stability and regulatory oversight remain critical.
 
🔐 Fraud is moving inside the customer relationship. TransUnion reports that 81% of digital fraud now targets existing accounts. This underlines a fundamental shift in financial crime, from fraudulent account creation towards account takeover and the exploitation of established customer trust.
 
The common thread? Technology is transforming finance faster than institutions can adapt their controls, governance and business models. Innovation creates opportunity, but without resilience, accountability and trust, it also creates new vulnerabilities.
